content: Beyond scheduling time for instruction and practice in all three areas of writing, teachers must know how to maximize that time. Effective writing instruction is more than assigning topics or practicing skills. It begins with Tier 1, whole-class, direct, and explicit teaching that sets students up for success. Educational research, including John Hattie's meta-analysis, underscores which practices most strongly influence student achievement. While nearly any writing instruction yields gains, direct and explicit instruction consistently has one of the greatest impacts on writing proficiency. Yet, even with this knowledge, many teachers remain uncertain about what explicit, direct instruction truly looks like. Clarifying this begins with understanding the differences between a mini-lesson and other forms of instruction.

In schools, almost anything that happens in the classroom can be called a lesson. Over time, the term has stretched to include a wide range of experiences — activities, discussions, work time, practice, explanations, directions, and assignments. Publishers have followed suit, labeling multiple components of their programs as the lesson. Not all lessons are the same. A lesson can take many forms, with each approach serving a distinct purpose in supporting student learning.

Student-Centered & Inquiry Approaches — PURPOSE: To promote curiosity, problem-solving, and deep understanding through active exploration and authentic tasks. TYPES:
• Inquiry-Based Learning — Students investigate questions or problems, building understanding through exploration and discovery.
• Project-Based Learning — Students engage in extended, real-world projects that integrate knowledge and skills from multiple areas.
• Experiential Learning — Students learn by doing, reflecting on hands-on experiences or simulations.
• Cooperative Learning — Students work together in small groups, with each member responsible for contributing to the group's success.

Discussion & Dialogue Approaches — PURPOSE: To encourage critical thinking, reasoning, and communication as students explore ideas collaboratively. TYPES:
• Discussion-Based Learning — Students learn through structured conversations, sharing ideas, evidence, and perspectives.
• Reciprocal Teaching — Students take turns leading a discussion using strategies like predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing.
• Socratic Seminar — A teacher-guided dialogue where students deepen understanding by asking and answering open-ended questions.

Flexible & Differentiated Approaches — PURPOSE: To meet diverse learning needs and preferences, allowing students to engage with content in ways that maximize growth. TYPES:
• Blended Learning — A mix of in-person teaching and online digital tools that allows for flexible, personalized learning.
• Differentiated Instruction — The teacher adapts content, process, or product to meet the diverse needs of learners.
• Flipped Learning — Content is introduced outside of class (often via video), while class time is used for practice and application.

Teacher-Directed Approaches — PURPOSE: To provide clear guidance and structured instruction to build concept/skill knowledge and know-how. TYPES:
• Content Instruction — The teacher delivers information lecture-style, with students listening, note-taking, and absorbing content.
• Direct Instruction — The teacher explicitly teaches skills or concepts step by step with clear modeling and guided practice.

While students can gain insights through peers, problem-solving, exploration, and experimentation, these approaches alone cannot teach writing effectively. Writing is not a skill students will figure out on their own — it must be taught via teacher-centered direct instruction. To further distinguish direct instruction from other types of lessons, educators use the term mini-lesson.

As Wolf (2007, cited in Graham, 2013) notes, "While learning to speak comes naturally to nearly all of us, writing is a largely unnatural skill that must be explicitly taught and learned." Individual writing skills require direct, explicit instruction that describes and demonstrates how to execute it successfully. The goal is to transfer the knowledge and the know-how from teacher to students so they can eventually apply the skill independently and consistently across future contexts.

Mini-lessons serve as the foundation of Tier 1 instruction, providing every student with clear, explicit teaching of essential grade-level writing skills. Without these lessons, students miss out on key instruction and struggle to meet grade-level standards. Omitting mini-lessons doesn't just slow learning — it actively limits students' opportunities to grow as writers.

Tier 1, whole-class, direct, explicit instruction means: core grade-level writing skill/standard, all students included, teacher-led thorough, clear, and precise explanation, teaching something new.

While mini-lessons are the core of Tier 1 writing instruction, research shows that many educators struggle to plan and deliver them successfully.

Research cited in The National Commission on Writing in America's Schools & Colleges (2003) shows that even experienced English Language Arts instructors often lack confidence in guiding students to write effectively, largely because they were not trained in HOW to teach it. Few states require courses in writing for teacher certification, leaving many without formal preparation. The irony is striking: educators are expected to develop skills in students that they themselves were never taught how to execute or model. Simply making time for instruction and practice (Essential #1) isn't enough. To truly improve student writing, schools must focus on teaching the teachers how to teach (Essential #2).

Educators need targeted professional development and resources that show how to plan and deliver direct, explicit mini-lessons in all three areas of writing — Language Foundations, Genre Writing, and Reading Response. Most weren't taught how to break a complex process — like crafting a strong introduction or organizing ideas logically — into clear, incremental steps that students can follow.

Professional learning must focus on HOW to translate writing expertise into teachable moments: how to name the skill, model it live, scaffold it appropriately, and release responsibility to students. Without this type of training, even experienced teachers will struggle to teach writing with clarity and confidence.

A mini-lesson is a brief, focused burst of instruction that launches every writing block. It follows a systematic structure to introduce and teach a grade-level writing skill. In just 10-15 minutes, the teacher explicitly introduces a single writing skill through a sequence of connected steps that begin the gradual release of responsibility.

This daily routine applies to all three areas of writing instruction — Language Foundations, Genre Writing, and Response Writing — each taught through the same 4-step mini-lesson structure followed by writing practice. Whether students are learning a convention, mastering a genre element, or responding to text, the mini-lesson provides the essential teaching before practice — because without new learning first, writers don't grow.

Step 1: Introduce. Begin by introducing a standards-based grade-level writing skill using its accurate academic vocabulary. Clearly name the skill and provide a sentence or two explaining what function the skill serves in writing. This is also when the trait language you've established in your classroom becomes valuable. Connect the skill to the broader writing trait it supports. This helps students organize new grade-level skills under one of the six overarching categories that define "good" writing. The power of this skill-to-trait connection comes later: when students receive feedback, they can link the skill to the trait, guiding their improvements.

When a mini-lesson is focused and narrow, introducing the skill should take no more than 30 seconds. This sets the stage for Step 2A, where the teacher will provide additional context.

Step 2A: Instruct. Spend the next one to five minutes providing key information about the new writing skill. Explain what the skill is and clarify its purpose or definition ("This skill..."). Explain why the skill matters and how it helps students become stronger, more effective writers ("It's an important skill because..."). Describe the genre, situations, or contexts in which the skill is applied, helping students see how it functions in real writing ("Writers use this when...").

In addition to background information about the skill, Step 2A may include showing strong and/or weak anchors. An anchor is a completed writing sample or an excerpt of mentor text that illustrates the skill in action. Strong anchors show the skill executed well, while weak anchors show the same skill performed poorly or missing entirely. Teachers often use weak anchors to demonstrate what writing looks and sounds like before the skill is included, and strong anchors to illustrate what it looks and sounds like after it's been addressed.

Besides providing key information and showing anchors, Step 2A also outlines a step-by-step process for how to incorporate the skill into one's writing. This is the heart of explicit instruction: telling students precisely how to do the skill in incremental steps so they can apply it whenever they write.

section_name: Step 2A: Universal Process and Anchor Charts
content:
The process described in Step 2A is not tied to a specific example or topic. It is a general process that can be applied to any topic. Step 2A focuses on a universal process for integrating the skill into writing, showing students how to execute it consistently across any context.

If explicit instruction is explained ONLY through an example, students risk understanding the skill in that one context but not knowing how to apply it elsewhere. The example is just that — an illustration of one of countless opportunities to use the skill. Without a general process explained in Step 2A, students lack the guidance to repeat the skill independently when faced with a different topic.

Consequently, this universal step-by-step process can be captured on a student-facing anchor chart. This timeless reference allows students to see and remember the process for executing the skill, providing guidance they can return to whenever they apply it — across any topic or context — helping ensure consistent, independent use over time.

Step 2A focuses on TELLING. It primes the learner's attention and gives him a framework to recognize and internalize the skill during the modeling phase. By explaining the purpose, function, and application of the skill in 2A, students gain the context needed to notice it within the teacher's modeled example in Step 2B. Step 2A takes 1-5 minutes. Step 2B occurs in the next 1-5 minutes.

Step 2B: Demonstrate. Step 2B is where the teacher executes the steps WHILE demonstrating the skill live. Teacher modeling is a hallmark of the Gradual Release of Responsibility framework (I Do, We Do, You Do). In Step 2B, the teacher demonstrates the skill alone. Graham (2019) and Marzano (2007) emphasize that effective instruction includes modeling, Think Alouds, and clear demonstrations of writing strategies and processes. During this phase — I do; you watch and listen — students simply observe, listen, and absorb how the skill is applied.

More than just performing the skill, the teacher provides a slow, intentional Think Aloud. She narrates her thought process as she works through the skill, unpacking the reasoning behind each choice. She's not talking to the students; she's talking to herself. She uses I, me, and my statements. The questions she asks are rhetorical; she answers them herself. It's a one-person monologue, where the teacher orally captions every step she takes when applying the skill.

The difference between telling about an example (Step 2A) and teaching through an example (Step 2B) lies in the Think Aloud. When teachers articulate their reasoning in real time, students gain access to expert decision-making. A lot of learning how to write well lives within the series of thoughts and decisions a writer makes.

The teacher's model in Step 2B focuses less on the skill itself and more on the writer's cognitive process — the very thinking that allows students to apply the skill independently and consistently. This is precisely what students need to observe and internalize. Students connect the general steps from Step 2A to the teacher's concrete example being created in front of them. THAT is the goal of a mini-lesson — to explicitly teach students how to execute a particular writing skill so that they can eventually replicate it.

Although students simply watch and listen for up to 10 minutes (1-5 minutes in Step 2A + 1-5 minutes in Step 2B), Step 3 invites their participation.

Step 3: Interact. Within the same mini-lesson, the teacher models the skill a second time, this time inviting students to join in orally. While this qualifies as a We Do, the teacher still carries most of the cognitive load. During these next several minutes, the teacher applies the skill in a second example, highlighting the same process detailed from Step 2A, and asking the same questions of herself — but pausing before giving "the answer."

Such moments are initiated when the teacher poses a whole-class question in Step 3 (e.g., "Let's look at another example. What transition word would best fit this situation?"). She then directs students to "turn and talk." Students immediately pivot to a peer and collaborate on an answer orally.

This guided interaction serves an important purpose: for students to execute the thinking process and orally participate in the steps the teacher outlined in Step 2A. Rather than calling on individuals, provide opportunities for all students to think through the skill's application. This includes time for students to Turn and Talk with a peer about how they might apply the skill. Teaching writing skills isn't about "doing" writing or applying a skill in a single written product. Teaching students how to write well requires teaching them decision-making processes they can apply within all future writing.

DISCLAIMER: Classrooms should absolutely include opportunities for students to discuss, ponder, consider, analyze, and generally pour over ideas. These much longer peer conversations do have a place in the classroom — but NOT in whole-class direct instruction. Students' guided attempts in Step 3 need to be efficient and effective and engage all students. The Turn & Talk strategy offers such an experience.

Step 3 of a direct-instruction mini-lesson is NOT an activity where students are coming up to the board or "doing" a class example. Within direct instruction, the teacher does not want to "share the pen" or call on individual students. These may be activities to do as whole-class practice AFTER the mini-lesson, but not during it.

Likewise, Step 3 is not a class discussion. Be careful not to give students too much time to turn and talk. It's a specific question that should cause students to quickly share their thoughts with a peer. If they don't have an answer, then they pivot to hear their peer's suggestion. Either way, in these instances, the Turn & Talk is only about 6-10 seconds long.

While students quickly share "answers" to the Turn-and-Talk questions, the teacher eavesdrops in order to massage, shape, and refine their ideas into a strong application of the skill. During Step 3 the teacher continues to hold the pen and will ultimately execute the skill in writing. Consequently, this We-Do in the mini-lesson is more accurately described as "I do again; you help a little."

Step 4: Close & Transition. Step 4 is only about 30 seconds and includes two components. First, restate the lesson's focus — the skill that was taught. Then describe the You-do task. Identify what you want students to do with that same skill during the practice time that will follow.

The mini-lesson is short because its purpose is to prepare students to write. It sets the stage, giving them the knowledge and context they need to practice the same skill within their own writing. Students don't improve during the mini-lesson — it's when they write afterward that real growth happens.

Direct, explicit instruction involves breaking tasks into manageable steps (Step 2A), providing clear guidance (Step 2B), and offering opportunities for both guided (Step 3) and independent practice (Step 4). Although the I Do and We Do happen within the 10-15 minute mini-lesson, the You-Do task is merely announced in the final 30 seconds or so. The actual execution of the You Do is done outside the 10-15 minute mini-lesson — during writing time.

Understanding the four-step architecture is one thing; executing it efficiently and effectively is another. Even the best mini-lessons fall flat without careful planning. Thoughtful planning transforms the four-step sequence into a powerful, consistent instructional tool. Without planning, a mini-lesson can quickly turn into improvisation.

Four key reasons planning matters:

1. Improve efficiency and focus. Mini-lessons should be truly mini — 15 minutes or less. Of that, only about 5 minutes is used to describe the new skill (Steps 1 and 2A); the rest is application (Steps 2B and 3). Careful planning keeps the lesson focused, purposeful, and aligned to the skill, ensuring a smooth, efficient delivery. Planning is like a dress rehearsal.

2. Maximize pacing and clarity. "Winging" a lesson often leads to tangents, forgotten steps, and lost learning. A plan keeps the lesson moving, maintains attention, and prevents muddled instruction. Scripted points — what to say, model, and reveal — allow teachers to stay on track and maintain students' focus.

3. Maintain teacher control. Without planning, teachers may pause too long during rhetorical questions or Think Alouds, prompting students to jump in and "help" before it's time. Step 2B is about modeling the thinking behind a skill, not producing an example with student assistance. If students intervene too early, the critical I-Do portion is lost.

4. Emphasize writer thinking. Without planning, Think Alouds can become vague or overgeneralized, reducing their instructional value. Because these writer actions are not obvious to students, teachers must engage in metacognition — pausing to think about their own thinking. Planning helps teachers slow down the automatic moves of expert writing to make those invisible decisions visible.

Writing time isn't about completing a task or writing product — it's about practicing the new skill as much as possible. This is the heart of the writing workshop: dedicated time for students to try, experiment, and repeat the skill within their own writing. Practice powers progress.

Writing time is when students attempt the skill on their own. They're no longer observing or helping the teacher — this is You-Do time. It's also when understanding — and misunderstanding — come to light. During the mini-lesson, everything sounds simple and looks easy. But applying a new skill to one's own writing is a complex process filled with choices and challenges.

Writing time is where students try new skills, make mistakes, and grow. This is often referred to as "the workshop." This in-class writing time is essential because it provides students with the opportunity to write regularly. Writing doesn't improve by listening to teachers and observing lessons. It evolves through consistent effort. Immediate application after every writing mini-lesson ensures students internalize the skill while teacher guidance is available.

It's important that each new skill is first practiced in class — not as homework or within independent stations. Students need real-time support from their teachers who can provide feedback, guide their efforts, and help them make informed writer decisions. When learners tackle a new skill for the first few times, the expert must be close at hand. During writing time, the teacher reads over shoulders and across screens. She circulates, confers, and answers questions.

One-on-one or small-group conversations — often called writer conferences — are essential for helping students navigate challenges and strengthen their skills. There are different types of conferences, each serving a distinct purpose.

Product Conferences: Often, conferring brings to mind a long, one-on-one meeting at the teacher's desk or a small table. This is a product conference, where the teacher spends 15-30 minutes with a single student reviewing all facets of a single genre-writing product. During a product conference, the teacher highlights the many strengths and areas for improvement, preparing the writing for a polished final draft.

While product conferences on genre-writing are valuable, they should be used sparingly — about three or four times per year. In between, teachers must hold shorter, more frequent conferences to support each writer's ongoing skill development in all 3 areas of writing — Language Foundations, Genre Writing, and Reading Response.

Process Conferences: Literacy expert Carl Anderson, in How's It Going?, identifies conferring as a teacher's most crucial role during writing time. Meeting with students while they write allows teachers to address challenges as they arise — rather than after a piece is finished. Conferring isn't about executing a skill in a single product; it's about helping students apply that skill across different contexts in all future writing.

Unlike a longer product conference, a process conference lasts just a few minutes and can occur at any stage of writing. By focusing on one or two targeted skills at a time, these short conferences provide digestible, actionable feedback, help teachers gauge where students are and what they need next, and allow them to meet with more writers each day.

End-of-unit product conferences are: individualized conversation, writing-focused, thorough (about the entire piece), summative (at the end of the writing process), long duration, and infrequent. Within-unit process conferences are: individualized or grouped conversation, writer-focused, targeted (about 1-2 skills), formative (during the writing process), short duration, and frequent.

When deciding what to focus on during a process conference, the 6 Traits provide a reliable guide. Since these six components represent the key characteristics of "good" writing at all levels and in all genres, make them the core of writer conferences.

The 6 Traits do more than define what "good" writing looks like — they provide a bridge between the teacher's instruction and students' practice. They connect what's taught in whole-class lessons to what students apply in their own drafts.

When conferring with a student, first compliment the trait(s) and skill(s) the student did well — this isn't a pat-on-the-head or "good job" statement. It's the teacher naming the skill executed well and encouraging the student to do it again in the future. Explain how the skill strengthens the communication of their ideas to the reader — even if it was unintentional. Highlight what they did well, reinforce the skill, and prompt them to intentionally repeat those 'accidental' writing choices in future drafts.

Effective writer feedback includes both strengths and next steps. While a teacher's instinct is often to offer many suggestions for improvement, a laundry list of things to fix will only overwhelm students. This overload of feedback is the key difference between simply fixing a student's writing and coaching them to become stronger, more independent writers. By focusing on one well-chosen comment, teachers can provide immediate, actionable feedback without overwhelming the student.

When prioritizing the one or two comments to share with a student, apply the concept of the "trophy" traits. Voice, word choice, and sentence fluency are valuable — they add sophistication and style to writing. However, the traits of Ideas, Conventions, and Organization are essential to the core message and carry more weight. While the stylistic traits polish the message, focus initial feedback on the "trophy" traits — those that impact the foundational content of the message.

Guidelines for prioritizing feedback:

1. Typically, the first consideration of genre-writing feedback is focused on the TRAIT OF IDEAS — reminding the writer of previously-taught writing skills that would make his writing stronger (by adding more meaningful details) and longer (through deeper development). This includes adding more vivid pictorial details, additional supporting sentences, or stronger evidence and elaboration.

2. However, if the student's ideas are difficult to read — whether because of handwriting or spelling — address readability before adding content. If more legible letter formation or handwriting is the problem, feedback centers around transcription skills and the TRAIT OF PRESENTATION. If spelling and phonics patterns impede the reader from gleaning the message, feedback should target the TRAIT OF CONVENTIONS.

3. Additionally, early writers — such as multilingual learners, pre-K through second graders, or students with special needs who primarily communicate through pictures — likely need to be encouraged to add more letters and words that match what they've drawn. Feedback should center on the TRAIT OF CONVENTIONS.

4. Finally, for writers whose ideas are readable and plentiful, assess that the text structure and flow of the details fits the genre and purpose they are writing. This feedback centers on the TRAIT OF ORGANIZATION — targeting logical order and appropriate transitions within the middle sentences and body paragraphs.

By connecting what the student did (or didn't do) in his writing with a trait and skill he has been taught, the teacher makes the feedback specific and actionable. Students aren't just told something is "good" or "needs work"; they are reminded of the exact skill to apply, why it matters, and how it strengthens their writing. The shared language of the 6 Traits also makes differentiation more manageable. While whole-class mini-lessons address grade-level skills, individual conferences target each student's immediate needs.

Teacher feedback isn't optional; it's essential. John Hattie's meta-analysis of over 900 studies found that "feedback was among the most powerful influences on achievement," with the most effective programs relying on frequent, targeted guidance. Through timely, focused conferences, students can master one skill at a time, gradually building stronger, more independent writers.

This clear, actionable feedback is not an endpoint; it's the beginning of a cyclical process: students attempt a skill in their writing, the teacher provides targeted feedback, the student revises based on that feedback, and the teacher observes the results to guide the next round of instruction and practice. This ongoing cycle of instruction, practice, and feedback is what John Hattie calls the feedback loop. It gradually equips students to apply their learning to future drafts with increasing confidence. As each skill strengthens, teachers can shift focus to new priorities in new pieces, creating continuous growth.

Action Steps for administrators and instructional leaders:

1. Provide targeted professional development. Build teachers' confidence and understanding of Tier 1 short, explicit mini-lessons by clarifying their purpose and structure versus other types of classroom lessons. Include modeling by professional consultants or teacher leaders to demonstrate the difference between telling students about a skill and teaching them how to execute it independently.

2. Implement a clear mini-lesson framework. Adopt the research-based four-step mini-lesson architecture — Introduce, Instruct, Interact, and Close — to ensure teachers plan and deliver short, focused lessons that model a single writing skill and make their thinking visible to students. Provide coaching and feedback that strengthen teachers' use of explicit instruction, insightful Think Alouds, and efficient Turn & Talks. Classroom observations should confirm efficient pacing, clear instructional purpose, and a gradual release of responsibility.

3. Verify practice follows instruction. Ensure students have dedicated, in-class time immediately after mini-lessons to practice newly taught skills. Classroom observations should show students actively applying the skill taught in the preceding 10-15 minute mini-lesson.

4. Monitor skill-focused writer conferences. Ensure teachers circulate during writing time to meet frequently with individual students or small groups for short, targeted conferences. Evidence includes documented conferences with a trait-based compliment and a suggested skill for improvement that focuses on a previously-taught skill of a high-impact "trophy trait" (ideas, conventions, or organization). Teachers articulate clear next steps, and students apply skills and transfer learning to new writing tasks.

5. Facilitate school-wide observation and reinforcement. Conduct follow-ups and coaching to maintain consistency in mini-lesson delivery, planning practices, and feedback cycles. Observation logs, coaching notes, or walkthrough forms show consistent execution of mini-lessons and writer conferences.

Step 2A worked example: Teaching young writers to add close-up picture details in informative writing.

This skill means adding little parts or details to the basic shapes in our drawings. These small details help the reader to see and understand more about our topic.

It's an important skill because the more close-up details we add, the more our reader learns about what the topic looks like and why it's special. The writer is able to communicate even more information with close-up picture details.

Writers use this when they want their picture writing to communicate small, important parts about the topic. This makes the topic come alive for the reader.

Step 2A also outlines a step-by-step process for how to incorporate the skill:

After drawing the basic shape(s) of the topic, the writer follows three steps:
1. ZOOM IN: The writer closes his eyes, imagines the topic, and "zooms in" on one area or part. Like a magnifying glass, he notices ONE close-up detail.
2. THINK: The writer opens his eyes and considers how to draw that small detail within his picture. He decides where to place it, what color to use, how big or small to make it, and whether to use straight lines, swirls, or dots. The writer knows he is teaching the reader and wants to draw the details correctly.
3. DRAW IT: The writer picks up his crayon, marker, or pencil and adds the close-up details as he imagined them.

After adding one close-up detail, the writer finds another part of the drawing and repeats the three steps.

Notice that the process described above is not tied to a specific example or topic. It is a general process that can be applied to any topic. Step 2A focuses on a universal process for integrating the skill into writing.

Step 2B worked example: Teacher models adding close-up details to a brown bear drawing via live think-aloud.

"Let's pretend I want to tell the reader about brown bears — a topic I know well." Reveal a basic drawing that includes the following all drawn with a brown crayon: an oval for the body, a circle for the head, and four skinny rectangles for legs.

Acknowledge that this basic drawing is a good start, but it's plain and has no close-up details. Reveal a color copy of the same bear where you will model how to add close-up details using the 3 steps: Zoom in, Think, Draw. Share your thinking while executing the steps.

1. ZOOM IN: "I'm going to close my eyes and 'zoom in' on one part of the bear — his face. I imagine a magnifying glass near his mouth. I notice something important: when a bear opens wide, it shows sharp, pointed teeth."

2. THINK: "I open my eyes and think to myself about how I could draw the teeth accurately. I know I can't draw a smiley face because that's not true. I have to draw the teeth so they are pointed. I ask myself — What shapes have points? Triangles! I'm going to draw many small pointy triangles."

3. DRAW IT: "Now I'm going to draw the bear's mouth with a row of small triangles to show that the bear has sharp teeth."

More than just performing the skill, the teacher provides a slow, intentional Think-Aloud. She narrates her thought process as she works through the skill, unpacking the reasoning behind each choice. She's not talking to the students; she's talking to herself. She uses I, me, and my statements. The questions she asks are rhetorical; she answers them herself. It's a one-person monologue, where the teacher orally captions every step she takes when applying the skill.

Step 3 worked example: Teacher guides students through adding more close-up details to the brown bear using Turn & Talk.

"Even though I've added close-up details to the mouth, I'm still not done. Help me find a second place to include more details about the bear using the same 3 steps: Zoom in, Think, Draw."

1. ZOOM IN: "Close your eyes and ZOOM IN on the bear's four legs. In your imagination, zoom in and look closely at his feet as if you had a magnifying glass. What do you see? Open your eyes and Turn & Talk."
"Back to me. I heard several of you say you imagined feet or paws at the end of a bear's legs."

2. THINK: "OK, now we have to THINK about how to draw those close-up details. What shapes? How big? What color? Turn & Talk."
"Back to me. I heard many of you say you'd draw a medium-sized oval for each paw."

3. DRAW IT: "So now we have to DRAW the paws. What color should we use? Say it together — 1, 2, 3, Blurt. I heard you say you would use your brown crayon."
"OK, I've got the brown marker. And where would you draw these ovals? Everybody, point in the air at our picture and show me where you would draw the ovals for paws. I'm seeing many of you pointing at the bottom of the bear's legs. OK, as I draw each paw with an oval, you draw it in the air with me."

After drawing the 4 paws, repeat the skill executing the same process with another set of close-up details.

1. ZOOM IN: "Close your eyes and ZOOM IN on the bear's four paws. In your imagination, zoom in and look closely at his feet as if you had a magnifying glass. What do you see? Open your eyes and Turn & Talk."
"Back to me. I heard several of you say you imagined sharp claws at the end of his paws."

2. THINK: "OK, now we have to THINK about how to draw those close-up details. What shapes? How big? What color? Turn & Talk."
"Back to me. I heard many of you say you'd draw several small triangles on the front of each bear paw to show he has pointy claws."

3. DRAW IT: "So now we have to DRAW the claws. What color should we use? Say it together — 1, 2, 3, Blurt. I heard some of you say you would use your brown crayon and others said their black crayon. Either of those would be great choices. But we wouldn't want to use a blue or purple crayon, because that's not true. And when we write informatively we always add accurate information for our readers."
"OK, I've got the black marker. Everybody, point in the air at our picture and show me where you would draw the small triangles for claws. I'm seeing many of you pointing at the side of the paw. OK, as I draw each sharp claw with a triangle, you draw it in the air with me."

Step 4 worked example: Closing the close-up picture details mini-lesson with a pumpkin independent writing task.

"Writers, today we learned a 3-step process for how to add close-up details to our own picture writing. By adding these little details, we can teach our readers even more about the topic we are writing about."

"For writing time, I'd like you to draw a pumpkin. We already know (from previous direct instruction) to start by drawing its basic shape and color. After that, I want you to add several close-up details using the 3-step process — Zoom in, Think, Draw (e.g., texture of pumpkin skin, stem, dirty spot from where it grew on the ground)."

"You get your crayons, and I'll pass out the paper. Let's go be writers!"
